children: To the Editor:  Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have expressed concern for humanity and the need for government stifling of artificial intelligence's development ("The World Isn't Ready for an Anthropic IPO," Cover Story, Sept. 17). The real question is whether the CEOs hope to protect their products subsequent to going public, or to hide their failures in developing AI safely prior to their initial public offerings.

To the Editor:  Anthropic's concerns about safety may be sincere, but that doesn't mean they're correct. Other AI leaders such as Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have said that many of those fears are unfounded. Safety versus cost is never a simple business decision. The implication that Anthropic might decide to forgo safety for a short-term return after it goes public seems highly unlikely. Government regulation is a risk, but it's highly unlikely that anything will get past the president's desk that significantly hinders the AI industry. It is one of America's greatest achievements, and it would be a shame if it becomes hobbled by unfounded fear mongering.

To the Editor:  If some catastrophe is heading our way, I'm betting that AI will figure out how to stop it ("Why OpenAI's Economist Is Bullish on Humans," Streetwise, Sept. 18). After all, if AI can do almost everything else, why not save the planet?

To the Editor:  The Federal Open Market Committee did the right thing in raising interest rates ("Higher Interest Rates Lead to More Inflation, Says This Economist. Take That, Central Bankers," Interview, Sept. 17). Now Congress needs to do the right thing and eliminate the annual deficit. This can be done by reducing spending and raising taxes to present a balanced budget. Once the annual deficits are eliminated and the government has a balanced budget, economic growth will whittle away at the national debt.

To the Editor:  Office real estate investment trusts, a tiny fraction of all REITs by market cap, all run debt to assets too high to be able to sustain their dividends across a recession ("The Office Boom Is Back. Can REITs Be Far Behind?" Sept. 15). And indeed, we have seen them all cut their dividends across the 2020s. You might manage to buy them low and sell them high, if you time this next cycle correctly. But income investors should just stay away.
